title: The body: clear knowing
hookLine: going and returning, looking, bending, dressing, eating, even in the toilet (MN 10)
last: THE BODY — I KNOW I'M SITTING.

lines: NO PART OF THE DAY LEFT OUT.
cards: Getting dressed. Chewing your food. Going to the toilet.

Not what anyone expects to hear about in a teaching on awakening. The Satipatthana Sutta lists them anyway, right in its instructions, next to walking, sitting and falling asleep. It isn't being crude.
It's making a point: there's no special room for this practice, no special hour, and no part of the day that doesn't count.

teach.b: Here's the list, in plain words. The practitioner acts with clear knowing when going forward and coming back. When looking ahead and looking away.
When bending and stretching a limb. When wearing the robe and carrying the bowl.
When eating, drinking, chewing and tasting. When relieving themselves. When walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking, and staying silent.

The word is sampajanna: clear knowing, or full awareness. Knowing what you're doing, and why, while you do it. It's the second word of the refrain you met five days ago, now with a whole section of its own.

The commentaries later unpacked it into four kinds: knowing the purpose of an action, knowing whether it's suitable, keeping it within the range of practice, and seeing it without the idea of a solid self behind it.
You don't need all four. The simple version is enough: you're there for it.

teach.h: THE WEEK: FROM BREATH TO EVERYTHING.
teach.b: Look back over this week and you'll see the path widening. Satipatthana: one way, four doors. Ardent and gentle.
The breath, known long and short, with skill. The chorus: inside and outside, arising and passing. The postures, the whole shape of the body.
And now clear knowing, the smallest actions of an ordinary day. The breath was one thread. The postures were four.

how: In many monasteries, clear knowing is practiced through daily chores, eating in silence, and slow, deliberate movement; lay practitioners often choose one routine act, like washing dishes, as a daily reminder.

o: knowing what you do, and why, while you do it
a calm mind gained only by sitting still
a deep trance that shuts out everyday life

games.q: match each action to the section it's from.
p: a long pull at the lathe

s: the sutta leaves bodily functions out as too ordinary
it lists eating, drinking, and relieving oneself: no part of the day is left out.
sampajanna is the second word of the sutta's refrain
the commentaries divide clear knowing into four kinds
purpose, suitability, range of practice, and seeing without a solid self.

games.q: you're brushing your teeth, planning tomorrow's meeting in your head. what would clear knowing do?
o: plan faster so you can focus later.
know the brushing while it happens: the taste, the motion, the purpose.
games.why: the sutta says clear knowing reaches every act, even the humblest ones.

practice: Slowly raise one hand and know it rising, turn the palm over and know it turning, lower it and know it lowering.
Turn your head a little to one side and back, bend a finger and stretch it, each small movement known while it happens. Then rest your hands and just sit, knowing you're sitting.

wordCard.voice: Sampajanna. Clear knowing: being there for the smallest actions of the day, from getting dressed to eating to the toilet.

orig.note: Pali sampajañña: clear knowing, full awareness of what you're doing and why.

carryVoice: Your line: even this. A dish, a toothbrush, a shoelace: all of it counts. That's day two hundred fifty-two.

sources.ref: Papañcasūdanī (commentary on MN 10), four kinds of clear knowing
